editorial.summary: A fan-compiled, Snapchat-era *Thumbs Up* travel record follows David Choe, Harry Kim and later Critter Fleming from San Francisco toward New York by rides, rail attempts and improvised hospitality. The compilation begins in the Castro on the day same-sex marriage is discussed, then crosses the Golden Gate Bridge and turns the search for a first ride into the season's operating pattern: prayer, provocation, mock commercials, songs, stranger interviews and repeated uncertainty about shelter and transportation. Marin and San Rafael lead toward Roseville rail yards, Reno and Salt Lake City. The group alternates hitchhiking with freight-train attempts, explaining enough mechanics to make the danger visible; the editorial layer does not convert those passages into a how-to. Drivers, families, fans, religious people, unhoused people, artists and hosts temporarily become the episode's center. The travelers trade clothes, eat in homes, debate religion and sexuality, gamble, argue and repeatedly ask what freedom, generosity and judgment mean on the road. Later sections move through Colorado and the Midwest to Chicago and Detroit, then Canada, Niagara Falls and New York. Critter's presence changes the group dynamic, while Harry's separation and return become an emotional through-line. The route is not a clean, official season master: it is a more than four-hour upload explicitly labeled as a Snapchat compilation, with inserted promos, repeated slogans, sleep audio, performance fragments and likely chronology gaps. The archive therefore treats it as one source route without pretending it proves a complete day-by-day itinerary. Much of the comedy uses racial, homophobic, religious, sexual and disability stereotypes, often while directly interviewing the people targeted. Those encounters are not evidence for the generalizations. Several moments also normalize unwanted touching, reckless driving, theft, trespass, drug use and dangerous rail behavior; warnings and restrictions preserve the record without endorsing it. The final New York movement reflects on imitation, projection and the end of a coast-to-coast journey while continuing the same abrasive public-performance style. Public participant names are corrected at route level; strangers and people identified only by first name remain private.
